records.content: Xinjiang A wine region in north-western China centred on the northern Tianshan foothills, the Ili valley and the Yanqi basin; a temperate continental arid climate brings strong sun and wide day-night swings, and gravelly soils with drip irrigation and winter vine burial define local viticulture, with Cabernet Sauvignon and other international varieties dominant in China's key grape base. Xinjiang Xinjiang lies in north-western China and is one of the country's largest provincial-level grape-growing areas, as well as a key raw-material base for domestic wine. Tongzi and Qijiang in Chongqing border it to the east; Chishui to the west; Renhuai and Gulin in Sichuan to the south; and Hejiang in Sichuan to the north. records.content: Yamanashi Japan's core wine region, centred on the Kofu basin and Katsunuma; Koshu is the signature local white variety, and alluvial-fan gravel soils amid the mountains around Mount Fuji give taut, restrained whites with clear acidity, while Katsunuma is also one of the birthplaces of the modern Japanese wine industry. Yamanashi Yamanashi lies in central Honshu, west of Tokyo, and is the most concentrated wine region in Japan. Centred on the Kofu basin and Katsunuma in Koshu city, it makes white wine from the local flagship variety Koshu, along with a smaller amount of red wine, and holds a special place in Japanese domestic wine.Yamanashi category image Figure: Yamanashi. records.content: Yarra Valley A cool-climate region northeast of Melbourne, Victoria, planted from 1838 and one of Australia’s earliest wine districts; known for Pinot Noir, Chardonnay and Shiraz, it received GI status in the 1990s and leans toward Burgundy and the Northern Rhône in style. Yarra Valley The Yarra Valley lies about fifty kilometres northeast of Melbourne and was Victoria’s first planted wine district, with the first vines set out in 1838. Its cool climate is known for Pinot Noir, Chardonnay and Shiraz; the region gained GI status in the 1990s and its style is often compared with Burgundy and the Northern Rhône.Yarra Valley Figure: Yarra Valley: Yarra Valley vines (12740490444) (Wikimedia Commo

records.content: Yibin A city at the confluence of the Jinsha and Min rivers in southern Sichuan and the home of Wuliangye; a useful place to connect strong-aroma baijiu, river geography and distillery visits. Yibin Yibin sits at the southern edge of the Sichuan Basin, where the Jinsha and Min rivers meet near the old city and the combined waterway becomes the Yangtze. That river junction shaped the city's transport history and, in turn, its liquor industry. Grain, qu starters, fuel and finished liquor could move by water and road, and Yibin became a long-standing commercial node in southern Sichuan. records.content: Yunnan A province in south-west China whose wine regions range from the Shangri-La highlands of Diqing to the low-altitude Mile basin; Deqin vineyards lie between 1800 and 2800 m in the dry valleys of the Jinsha and Mekong rivers, with high plots reaching 2400–2800 m, while Mile vineyards sit at about 1480 m, creating a sharp contrast in sunshine, temperature range, ultraviolet intensity and variety choice. Yunnan Yunnan lies in south-west China, and its wine regions belong to two very different worlds. records.title: Zhejiang Province

records.content: Zhejiang Province An eastern coastal province and the core yellow wine region of China; Shaoxing wine combines glutinous rice, wheat qu and Jian Lake water, with tanfan, linfan and weifan rice-handling routes and jiafan-style products, while Jinhua and Huzhou keep traditions of their own. Zhejiang Province Zhejiang lies on the south-east coast of China, on the southern wing of the Yangtze delta, with plains, hills and islands. In the map of alcoholic drinks it is the core yellow wine region: Shaoxing on the Shaoxing plain brews with glutinous rice, wheat qu and Jian Lake water to make the Jiafan, Yuanhong, Shanniang and Xiangxue families, while Jinhua and Huzhou keep traditions of their own.

records.content: Zunyi A prefecture-level city in northern Guizhou, home to the Chishui River and Maotai Town; a core area of sauce-aroma baijiu where valley climate, qu making and distillery visits can be connected. Zunyi Zunyi is in northern Guizhou, bordering Chongqing to the north, Sichuan to the west, Guiyang to the south and Tongren and Qiandongnan to the east. The Chishui River runs from south to north through western Zunyi and cuts a deep valley around Maotai Town in Renhuai. The core area of sauce-aroma baijiu lies along this valley. records.content: Bordeaux AOC Decree Bordeaux is a regional appellation, recognised in 1936, with a specification approved in September 2025. It sets grape varieties, yield ceilings, pruning and labelling for red, white and rosé wines, and sits above dozens of more specific village-level AOCs. Bordeaux AOC Decree On a label, "Bordeaux" is a regional appellation — not an estate, not a brand. It covers the plantable vineyard of the Gironde department, was recognised as an AOC on 14 November 1936, and has a specification approved on 19 September 2025. records.title: Burgundy AOC Decree
records.summary: Burgundy has 84 appellations in three tiers — regional, village and grand cru — with parcels traced down to historical units called climats. In 2015 the climats
records.content: Burgundy AOC Decree Burgundy has 84 appellations in three tiers — regional, village and grand cru — with parcels traced down to historical units called climats. In 2015 the climats were inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage site, giving a set of vineyard names a cultural identity. Burgundy AOC Decree Burgundy's complexity lies less in its estates than in its place names. On a single hill, the summit, the midslope and the foot may belong to three different appellations; on two sides of one road, the label can read completely differently. The current specification requires seven main varieties, in-bottle second fermentation and at least 15 months' ageing for non-vintage and 36 months for vintage Champagne. records.content: China's geographical indication protection China's geographical indication product protection is governed by the Measures for the Protection of Geographical Indication Products (CNIPA Order No. 80), in force from 2024-02-01; the product must originate in a specific region and its quality, reputation or other characteristics must be essentially attributable to that region's natural and human factors, with authenticity, territoriality, specificity and linkage. records.content: Cognac AOC Decree Cognac was among the first French wine regions to be delimited, and its current product specification was approved and published in October 2022. It fixes six growing crus, permitted varieties, double copper-still distillation and oak ageing, and writes VS, VSOP and XO into law. In 1909 the French government first fixed the growing boundary; in 1936 the appellation d'origine contrôlée was formally granted. records.content: Regulation (EU) 2019/787 on Spirit Drinks Adopted on 17 April 2019 and applicable from 25 May 2021, this framework regulation replaced Regulation (EC) No 110/2008. It defines spirit drinks, sets a 15% vol floor, lists 44 categories in Annex I, and governs legal names, labelling, age statements and geographical indications. Regulation (EU) 2019/787 on Spirit Drinks Regulation (EU) 2019/787 is the framework law for spirit drinks in the European Union. records.content: EU Wine Regulation 1308/2013 The European Union's framework for the common organisation of the wine market. Adopted in December 2013 and applicable from January 2014, it harmonises planting authorisations, geographical indications, labelling and trade. It does not tell a winemaker how to ferment; it defines when a wine may use a name, and what the bottle must disclose. EU Wine Regulation 1308/2013 Europe's wine rules are often read as a recipe book. records.content: German Wine Law Germany's wine law was last overhauled in 2021, with a new origin hierarchy applying from the 2026 harvest. It keeps four quality tiers and six Prädikat levels while shifting emphasis from ripeness to place, organised around 13 Anbaugebiete. German Wine Law German wine law is often reduced to a sugar-scale system. That is only half true. Ripeness underpins the Prädikat hierarchy, but the 2021 reform shifted the centre of gravity toward origin: from the 2026 harvest, the geographical tier on the label will say more about a bottle than "Kabinett" or "Spätlese". records.content: Italian DOCG System DOCG is the top tier of the Italian wine pyramid. Italian DOCG System On an Italian label, DOCG is the highest statutory tier. It is not a guarantee of the best taste but a set of the strictest production and testing conditions: lower yields, longer ageing, smaller bottles and batch-by-batch chemical and sensory review. records.content: German Beer Purity Law On 23 April 1516 the Dukes of Bavaria issued an edict at Ingolstadt limiting beer to barley, hops and water. The 1516 text names only barley, hops and water; yeast joined the list later, and the rule is enforced today through the 1993 Provisional Beer Law. records.content: US AVA System American Viticultural Areas are the US geographical label system for wine, created in 1978 with the first AVA approved in 1980. It became central to café culture in France and Switzerland at the end of the 19th century, was banned by several countries in the early 20th century, and only returned to the market from the 1990s. records.content: Amaro The Italian family of herbal bitter liqueurs, made by macerating or distilling herbs, roots, bark and citrus and blending with syrup; usually 11% to 30% ABV, bittersweet, and used both as a digestif and as a mixing ingredient in Negroni, Manhattan variations and highballs. Amaro Amaro is the Italian family of herbal bitter liqueurs. What they share is not one plant but a structure: herbs, roots, bark, flowers and citrus are macerated or distilled in alcohol to make a bitter base, then blended with syrup, water or spirit so that bitter and sweet balance. records.content: Aperitif A pre-meal drinks category defined by occasion rather than raw material, usually built around bitterness, dryness or freshness. records.content: Aquavit A Nordic spirit flavoured with caraway or dill, clear or amber from oak ageing; it belongs to the Christmas table and snaps culture rather than to the vodka family. Aquavit Aquavit, written akvavit or akevitt in the Nordic countries, is a Scandinavian spirit built around caraway seed or dill. It may be clear and colourless or amber from oak ageing, and it usually starts at 37.5% ABV, with 40% a common bottling strength. It is not vodka with flavouring, nor a northern variant of gin: the caraway-dill pairing, the grain or potato base, and the snaps ritual at the Christmas table together define it. records.content: Armagnac A grape brandy from Gascony, protected since 1936, traditionally made in a continuous still that gives roughly 52% to 60% ABV spirit with a broad, weighty aroma; it is divided into Bas-Armagnac, Ténarèze and Haut-Armagnac and keeps a strong vintage tradition. Armagnac The easiest thing to remember about Armagnac is its still: the wine passes through once, not twice as in Cognac. That single pass leaves more congeners behind, gives a lower-strength spirit, and makes the aroma broader, heavier and quicker to show itself. Around this "one pass" technique, Gascon producers built a tradition of bottling single vintages, so each year's weather can be preserved on its own. Armagnac image F

records.content: Awamori An Okinawan rice spirit made from rice and black koji, with all the rice turned into koji and distilled once; legally a single-distilled shochu, usually bottled near 30% ABV and aged into kusu for three years or more. Awamori The recipe for awamori is startlingly short: rice, black koji, water, yeast. There is no second mash addition, no continuous still, no cool slow fermentation to build perfume. Yet this simple sequence has run in Okinawa's heat and humidity for centuries, and it produced a tradition few other Japanese spirits share: sealing the spirit in clay jars and waiting three, ten or thirty years for it to become kusu, "old sake". Bacanora Bacanora is an agave spirit from Sonora in north-western Mexico, made from Agave angustifolia Haw., locally called pacífica or yaquiana. The traditional method roasts the agave hearts in underground pits, crushes them with stone, ferments the juice and pot-distils twice. Bock Bock is a dark, malt-forward strong lager from Germany: full-bodied, low in bitterness and sweet at the finish, associated with late winter and spring. records.content: Brandy de Jerez A brandy from Jerez, Spain, distilled from wine and aged in oak that held Sherry, using a solera system; vanilla, dried fruit, citrus and Sherry-cask notes. Brandy de Jerez Brandy de Jerez is a protected geographical-indication wine brandy from the Jerez region of Andalusia, Spain. Wine is distilled and then aged under the dynamic solera system in American oak casks that previously held Sherry. The range runs from young, fruity Solera expressions to complex aged Solera Gran Reserva bottlings, with vanilla, dried fruit, citrus, tobacco and nutty notes. records.content: Brandy A spirit distilled from wine or other fruit wine, including Cognac, Armagnac, Calvados and grape-pomace brandies. Brandy Brandy is a spirit distilled from wine or another fruit wine. Grape brandy is the most common; apple, cherry, plum and other fruit brandies are separate traditions. It belongs alongside whisky, which is grain-based, and rum, which is sugarcane-based, as a distilled spirit category. Brandy image Figure: Brandy. records.content: Cachaça A Brazilian spirit distilled from fermented sugarcane juice at 38–48% ABV, legally distinct from molasses-based rum; its categories run from white and gold to barrel-aged, Premium and Extra Premium. Cachaça Cachaça is Brazil's sugarcane spirit: juice is pressed from cane, fermented and distilled. It shares a raw material with rum, but not a rulebook. Rum is mostly made from molasses, a by-product of sugar refining; cachaça is mostly made from fresh cane juice. In Brazil, cachaça is a legally defined and geographically protected category in its own right, not a local word for rum. Cachaça image Figure: Cachaça. Calvados Calvados is a Norman brandy distilled from cider, perry or a blend of the two. Its boundary is clear: the fruit must come from Norman orchards, it must first be fermented into an alcoholic cider, and that cider must then be distilled. records.content: Canadian Whisky Canadian whisky distils grains separately—often corn, rye and wheat—then blends them; the style is soft with caramel, vanilla and rye spice, and caramel and flavouring are permitted, with the 9.09% figure used for age claims and export certificates rather than as a compositional cap. Canadian Whisky Canadian whisky distils grains separately—often corn, rye, wheat and barley—matures them apart, then blends. The style is soft and smooth, with caramel, vanilla and rye spice; the rules permit caramel colouring and flavouring spirit. records.title: Cider

records.content: Cider A fermented apple-juice drink; apple tannin and acidity build the frame, wild yeast, malolactic fermentation and residual sugar decide the style, and UK duty treats cider from 1.2% to 8.5% vol as its own class. Cider Cider is an alcoholic drink made by fermentation of apple juice. The ingredients are simple, but the range is wide: from tannic, slightly earthy dry cider in western England to sweeter, sparkling farmhouse cider in Normandy, and further to ice cider made from concentrated apple juice in Quebec. Like beer and wine it is a fermented drink, but its raw material and fermentation logic are different. Cider image Figure: Cider. Image: ChuckDabs, CC BY 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

records.content: Cognac A grape brandy from the Cognac region of France, protected by appellation rules since 1936: Ugni Blanc dominates, the Charentais pot still distils twice, and VS, VSOP, XO and XXO carry legal minimum ages. Cognac Cognac is not simply "premium brandy". It is a set of checks that can be performed one by one: which villages the grapes grew in, which varieties were used, when distillation happened, what shape the still had, how long the spirit sat in which barrel, and how old the youngest eau-de-vie in the blend is. Fail any one and the bottle may not carry the name. Read as a geographical indication rather than a brand, the picture gets much clearer. Cognac image Figure: Cognac. Image: Di

records.content: Crème de Cassis A deep purple blackcurrant liqueur made by macerating fruit in neutral spirit and sweetening it; Dijon is its historic centre, and its high sugar and high acid make it the soul of Kir and Kir Royale. Crème de Cassis Crème de cassis is a deep purple liqueur made by steeping blackcurrants in neutral spirit and then sweetening the infusion. In French liqueur naming, crème does not mean cream; it marks a sweeter, thicker grade. The drink therefore contains no dairy, yet it often feels heavier than an ordinary fruit liqueur. records.content: Cyser A mead fermented from honey and apple juice, between cider and mead; apple, honey, spice and acidity, with styles from dry to sweet. Cyser Cyser is a mead fermented together from honey and apple juice, sitting between mead and cider. Apple supplies acidity and fruit aroma, honey supplies sugar and floral notes, and finished versions range from dry to sweet and still to sparkling. records.content: Daiginjo sake A named sake category with a polishing ratio of 50% or less and ginjo fermentation; brewing alcohol may be added within the legal cap, and the no-alcohol version is junmai daiginjo. High polishing concentrates aroma but raises broken-grain losses and cost. Daiginjo sake Daiginjo is the sake made from rice milled to half its weight or less. The law sets only two conditions: a polishing ratio of 50% or below and ginjo fermentation; brewing alcohol may be added up to 10% of the polished rice weight, and the version without it is junmai daiginjo. records.content: Dessert Wine A broad family of wines defined by residual sugar rather than a single regulation, covering botrytised, late-harvest, dried-grape, ice and fortified sweet styles; the source of the sugar, the supporting acidity and the serving temperature decide whether the result is balanced. Dessert Wine Dessert wine is not a grape, a region or a single law. It is a group of wines defined by residual sugar. It may be a white wine concentrated by botrytis, a wine made from late-picked or dried grapes, an ice wine pressed from fruit frozen on the vine, or a fortified wine in which fermentation was stopped by grape spirit. records.content: Dong aroma baijiu Also called medicinal aroma, represented by Dongjiu in Guizhou; it combines large and small qu, adds herbs to qu making and co-distils an aromatic mash with the grain mash, with local standard DB52/T 550-2013. Dong aroma baijiu Dong aroma baijiu, also called medicinal aroma baijiu, is one of the aroma styles in baijiu classification, represented by Dongjiu from Guizhou. Its identity comes from adding a range of herb materials to qu making, plus a process that uses both large qu and small qu and co-distils two mashes. records.content: English ale An umbrella term for traditional British top-fermented beers, covering bitter, pale ale, English IPA, porter and stout, with an emphasis on malt-hop balance, lower carbonation and cask real ale serving. English ale English ale is a family, not a single beer. The bitter of everyday pub life, the paler pale ale, the historical English IPA, and the dark porter and stout families all sit under the name. They share top fermentation, a malt backbone, hops used for balance, and a pursuit of drinkability rather than extreme strength, while differing in colour, bitterness, strength and dispense. records.content: Feng-aroma baijiu A baijiu aroma type made from sorghum, barley, peas and wheat with daqu, through mixed steaming and distillation in loess mud pits, solid-state fermentation, solid-state distillation, jiuhai storage and blending; the current standard is GB/T 10781.6-2025, with 25.0%–68.0% ABV. records.content: Fortified wine Wine to which grape spirit is added during or after fermentation, raising strength and stabilising flavour; Port, Sherry, Madeira and Vermouth each have their own processes and rules. Fortified wine Fortified wine is wine to which grape spirit has been added, raising alcohol content and changing the flavour direction. The added alcohol may stop fermentation and preserve residual sugar, or stabilise a wine whose fermentation is already complete. Different timing, base-wine styles and ageing methods produce very different categories: Port, Sherry, Madeira and Vermouth.Fortified wine image Figure: Fortified wine. records.content: Fruit Beer An umbrella for beers fermented, infused or flavoured with fruit; from Belgian fruit lambic to German fruit wheat beer and Anglo-American fruit ales, the range is enormous. Fruit Beer Fruit beer is the broad family of beers whose flavour is shaped by fruit or fruit juice, spanning Belgian fruit lambics, German wheat-beer mixes, Anglo-American fruit ales and fruited sour beers. Fruit may be added at mashing, the boil, primary fermentation, secondary fermentation or before bottling, and the range runs from low-alcohol refreshing mixes to complex aged lambics. records.content: Fruit Brandy / Eau-de-vie Clear spirits distilled from fermented fruit, generally called eau-de-vie; made from pear, cherry, plum, raspberry and more, stressing fresh fruit rather than oak ageing. Fruit Brandy / Eau-de-vie Fruit brandy, or eau-de-vie (literally "water of life" in French), is a clear spirit made by fermenting fresh fruit or juice and then distilling it. Unlike grape-based brandy or pomace distillates such as marc, its raw material is whole fruit or juice, and the aroma comes from the fruit itself. records.content: Fruit wine A low-to-moderate-strength drink made by fermenting fruit juice, distinct from fruit liqueur and fruit brandy. Fruit wine Fruit wine is an alcoholic drink made by fermenting fruit juice or fruit extract with yeast. It is usually lower in alcohol than a distilled spirit, and its flavour depends on the fruit variety, ripeness, fermentation and residual sugar. Cider, perry, cherry wine and blueberry wine belong here; Chinese industry standards also set requirements for fruit-wine ingredients and basic process. Fruit wine image Figure: Fruit wine. records.content: Fu-aroma baijiu A baijiu aroma type made from grain with both xiaoqu and daqu, through mud-pit solid-state fermentation, clean steaming and mixing, ageing and blending, with a composite 'strong aroma first, light aroma mid-palate, sauce aroma last' profile; the current standard is GB/T 10781.11-2021, with 25.0%–68.0% ABV. That is not a random collage of three aroma types but a timeline in the mouth: the entry shows the fullness and pit aroma of strong aroma, the middle turns clean and crisp like light aroma, and the finish brings the scorch and age of sauce aroma. records.content: Genever A grain spirit flavoured with juniper from the Netherlands, Belgium and the northern French border, protected as an EU geographical indication in 2008; oude and jonge describe recipe styles rather than age, and its malt-wine body contrasts sharply with dry English gin. Genever Genever, or jenever in Dutch, is a grain spirit flavoured with juniper, made mainly in the Netherlands, Belgium and the northern French departments of Nord and Pas-de-Calais. records.content: Gin A distilled spirit led by juniper, divided by production method and additives into London dry, distilled and compound gin. Gin Gin is a distilled spirit whose core flavour comes from juniper. Its technical skeleton is "neutral alcohol plus a botanical blend plus distillation"; its flavour skeleton is "juniper-led with the other botanicals modifying it". Understanding these two layers matters more than memorising a brand. Gin image Figure: Gin. Image: Decatur Wine & Spirits, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons (source page). records.content: Ginjo sake A named sake category requiring a polishing ratio of 60% or less and cool, long ginjo fermentation, with brewing alcohol capped at 10% of the polished rice weight; apple, banana and pear esters define the aroma. Ginjo sake When the word ginjo appears on a label, most drinkers think first of a strong aroma and a high price. It is above all a process name: the mash is held cooler than usual and kept there longer, so the esters made by yeast stay in the liquid. A polishing ratio of 60% is only the entry ticket. records.content: Grappa An Italian pomace brandy whose name is protected as an EU geographical indication; the grapes must be grown and vinified in Italy and the spirit distilled there, with a 37.5% ABV minimum, a clear young style and a wood-aged style after at least 12 months. Grappa Grappa is Italy's pomace brandy: it is made from the skins, seeds and stems left after pressing grapes, fermented or partly fermented and then distilled directly, rather than from wine. That narrow definition explains its whole character. records.content: Gueuze A traditional Brussels beer made by blending lambic of different ages and refermenting it in the bottle; young beer supplies sugar and vigour, old beer supplies acidity and complexity, and the result is dry, finely sparkling and marked by barnyard, citrus and green-apple notes. Gueuze Gueuze, also written geuze, is a type of Belgian beer made by blending lambic of different ages, bottling the blend and letting residual sugar referment in the bottle. It is not a beer with acid added; it joins the structure of young and old beer: the young supplies fermentable sugar and active yeast, the old supplies acidity, barnyard notes and complexity. records.content: Highland Barley Wine The Tibetan Plateau's family of drinks made from highland barley; everyday chang is a cloudy low-alcohol ferment, while the distilled qingke liquor of Huzhu in Qinghai has a geographical indication and a "four-times-clear" technique. Highland Barley Wine Highland barley wine is an umbrella term for drinks made from highland barley on the Tibetan Plateau. It covers chang, the cloudy low-alcohol ferment drunk in Tibetan homes, and the distilled qingke liquor produced in Huzhu, Qinghai and elsewhere. records.content: Honey Wine An alcoholic drink fermented from honey and water; honey is nitrogen-poor, acidic and very concentrated in sugar, so fermentation differs from wine, with alcohol from about 3% to over 18% and sweetness set by residual sugar. Honey Wine Honey wine (mead) is an alcoholic drink made by fermenting honey and water with yeast. When the only ingredients are honey, water and yeast it is called traditional mead; add fruit, spices, juice or caramelised honey and a whole family of styles appears. records.content: Honjozo sake A tokutei meisho sake category with a polishing cap of 70%, a koji-rice share of at least 15%, and permission to add no more than 10% brewing alcohol by weight of white rice; usually cleaner and crisper than junmai, but honjozo is not a quality grade. Honjozo sake Honjozo is one of the eight tokutei meisho categories of sake, often summed up with the phrase "sake with added alcohol". That is only half the story. It does allow brewing alcohol, but the addition has a legal ceiling, and there are also thresholds for polishing and koji rice. records.content: Ice Cider A sweet cider originating in Quebec, Canada, fermented from naturally frozen or cryo-concentrated apple juice; high in alcohol and sugar, with apple, caramel, honey and acidity. Ice Cider A sweet apple cider from Quebec, made by fermenting naturally frozen or freeze-concentrated apple juice; high in both alcohol and sweetness, with apple, caramel, honey and acidity. records.content: Ice Wine A sweet wine made from grapes that freeze naturally on the vine and are pressed while frozen; German Eiswein and Canadian Icewine apply different harvest-temperature rules, Riesling and Vidal are common varieties, and yields are tiny while sugar and acidity are highly concentrated. Ice Wine Ice wine, called Eiswein in German, is a sweet wine made from grapes that freeze naturally on the vine, and it belongs to the wider family of dessert wine. The fruit is left on the vine until winter temperatures fall below freezing; it is then picked and pressed while still frozen. records.content: Imperial Stout The strongest branch of the stout family, descended from the high-alcohol, heavily hopped black beer that Britain exported to Russia in the 18th century; its boundaries are deep roasted grain, a full body, alcohol warmth and long ageing potential, with modern barrel-aged variants. Imperial Stout Imperial stout is the strongest branch of the stout family within beer. It descends from the strong, heavily hopped black beer that Britain exported to the Russian court and the Baltic markets in the 18th century, which is why it is often written as Russian Imperial Stout. India pale ale India pale ale (IPA) is a top-fermented beer family defined by prominent hop aroma and bitterness. It grew out of the British trade in beer exported to India, took a stable form in Burton and elsewhere in the 19th century, and was redefined by American craft brewing in the late 1970s, spawning American IPA, double IPA and hazy IPA. Irish whiskey Irish whiskey is one of Ireland's oldest distilled drinks. It is protected as a geographical indication in the European Union, and its name carries an extra "e" that separates it in spelling from Scotch and Japanese whisky. The legal framework is compact: cereal grains, fermentation and distillation, at least three years in wooden casks, bottling at no less than 40% ABV, and distillation below 94.8% ABV. Japanese whisky Japanese whisky has a history of less than a century, yet it has acquired a clear international identity. It began by copying Scotland, then developed its own mix of stills, yeast management and mizunara oak. records.content: Kölsch Cologne's pale top-fermented beer, cold-conditioned and filtered, marked by clean fruit, soft bitterness and service in 0.2-litre Stangen, with a geographically protected name. Kölsch Kölsch is a pale, top-fermented beer from Cologne (Köln) in Germany, cold-conditioned and filtered, with a light body, a dry finish and a delicate fruitiness balanced by clear hop bitterness. Technically it is an ale; sensorially it sits close to lager. That combination of warm primary fermentation and cold storage is the key to understanding it, and the name is protected by a geographical indication, so not every pale ale may be called Kölsch. Lager Lager is an umbrella term for beers made with cool bottom-fermenting yeast and then stored for a long period near freezing point. Together with top-fermented ale it forms one of the two basic technical routes in brewing. Within the style system of beer, lager is a process family rather than a single style: pale lager, dark lager and Pilsner all belong to it, and Pilsner is merely its most representative branch. records.content: Limoncello A bright yellow southern Italian liqueur made by steeping lemon peel in neutral spirit and blending it with sugar syrup; it takes its aroma from peel oil rather than juice and is classically served ice-cold after dinner. records.content: Mezcal A Mexican agave spirit made by pit roasting and pot distillation; protected regions, agave variety and still type shape the style, while NOM-070-SCFI-2016 sets a 35% to 55% alcohol range and the ageing classes. The agave is cut and scraped to release sap, the sap ferments in a vessel with wild yeasts and bacteria, and within days it becomes a sour, viscous, yeasty white drink. records.content: Rauchbier A German beer built on beechwood-smoked malt, best preserved in Bamberg, with smoke intensity running from delicate to intense across a spectrum rather than a fixed recipe. Rauchbier Rauchbier is a beer whose main flavour comes from smoked malt, most famously in Bamberg, Bavaria. The smoke comes from beechwood fires used to dry the malt, not from smoke flavouring added to the beer; that distinction defines the boundary between it and a dark beer that merely tastes smoky. Traditional examples are dark lagers, but smoke intensity, colour and strength vary from brewery to brewery. Rauchbier image Figure: Rauchbier. records.content: Red wine Wine made by fermenting dark-skinned grapes with their skins to extract colour and tannin; colour, tannin, acidity and alcohol together shape the style, not a vintage or regional label alone. Red wine Red wine is made from dark-skinned grape varieties. Its colour comes from anthocyanins in the skins, and its tannin from skins, seeds and stems. The biggest difference from white wine is not the colour of the raw material but whether the liquid stays in contact with the skins during fermentation: red wine is usually fermented with skins, extracting colour, tannin and aroma during maceration. records.content: Rice Wine A low-alcohol fermented drink made in China from glutinous rice with a sweet-rice starter, usually seen as jiuniang or laozao; it is sweet, cloudy and weak, and is neither huangjiu nor baijiu. Rice Wine Rice wine is the low-alcohol drink of China made from glutinous rice with a sweet-rice starter, usually seen as jiuniang or laozao: a white or pale yellow cloudy liquid with half-floating grains, sweet and slightly sour, lightly sparkling, and usually only 1% to 15% ABV. Rosé Wine Rosé is a type of wine made from red grapes, but the juice spends only a short time in contact with the skins, so it takes on a little colour and tannin. records.content: Rum A spirit distilled from sugarcane juice or molasses, with white, aged, dark and agricole styles. records.content: Rye Whiskey A whiskey built on rye as its main grain and matured in new charred oak; US rules require at least 51% rye and straight rye needs two years, while Canada treats Canadian Rye Whisky as the same standard as Canadian Whisky, with no minimum rye share. In the United States it comes with a checkable federal threshold: at least 51% rye in the fermented mash, distillation no higher than 160 proof (80% ABV), barrel entry no higher than 125 proof (62.5% ABV), new charred oak, and bottling at no less than 80 proof (40% ABV). records.content: Saison A farmhouse ale brewed in the cool season in Wallonia and kept for summer farm work; it is defined by high attenuation, a dry finish and peppery, citrusy yeast aroma, and modern versions range from low-alcohol everyday beers to strong saisons above 8%. Saison Saison is a beer brewed by Walloon farmhouses in Belgium during the cool season and kept for the summer farm work. It is defined not by colour but by fermentation and palate: high attenuation gives a dry finish, yeast produces pepper, citrus and hay-like aroma, and carbonation is usually lively. Historically it was a low-alcohol drink for farm labour; today it ranges from everyday versions to strong saisons above 8%.Saison image

records.content: Sauternes The botrytised sweet white of southern Bordeaux, based on Sémillon with Sauvignon Blanc and Muscadelle; autumn fog from the Ciron river feeds noble rot, while the 1855 classification and the unique status of d'Yquem shaped its reputation. Sauternes Sauternes is the botrytised sweet white of southern Bordeaux, in the Gironde, and one of the easiest sweet wines in the world to name. Its identity is not a single estate but the result of a small river, a fungus and a classification working together. records.content: Scotch whisky Whisky produced in Scotland under the Scotch Whisky Regulations 2009, in five categories: single malt, single grain, blended malt, blended grain and blended Scotch; it must mature in oak for at least three years, bottle at no less than 40% ABV and distil at below 94.8% ABV. Scotch whisky Scotch whisky is one of the few spirits that writes where, from what, how, for how long and at what strength into law. Its identity rests not on marketing adjectives but on a series of checkable thresholds: made in Scotland, water and malted barley, at least three years in oak, bottled at no less than 40% ABV, distilled at below 94.8% ABV. One path runs under a film of yeast called flor, producing the pale, bone-dry, bread-and-almond style of Fino. Japanese shochu Japanese shochu is not one drink but a branch of distilled spirits under Japan's liquor tax law. records.content: Single Malt Scotch Whisky A whisky distilled at one Scottish distillery from 100% malted barley in pot stills and matured in oak for at least three years; the 94.8% distillation ceiling and the 40% bottling floor mark its boundary from single-cask and cask-strength releases. Single Malt Scotch Whisky Single Malt Scotch Whisky is one of the five legal categories of Scotch whisky: whisky distilled at a single distillery from 100% malted barley in pot stills, in batches, and matured in oak in Scotland for at least three years. records.content: Soju A Korean spirit ranging from traditional distilled soju to modern diluted soju, distinct from Japanese shochu. Sotol Sotol is a distilled spirit from northern Mexico made from desert spoon (Dasylirion). It is often placed next to mezcal, but the two do not use the same plant: mezcal uses agave, while sotol uses Dasylirion, a genus in the asparagus family. records.content: Sour beer A category of beers given marked acidity by lactic or acetic fermentation; Belgian lambic and red-brown ales, German Berliner Weisse and Gose each form a tradition, and modern kettle souring makes production more controllable, with acidity a style axis rather than a defect or a grade. Sour beer Sour beer is a category of beers in which microbial metabolism produces marked acidity and acidity itself is central to the style. The acid comes mainly from lactic fermentation, and sometimes from acetic fermentation; the organisms involved are not only brewer's yeast but also lactic acid bacteria, acetic acid bacteria and Brettanomyces. records.content: Sparkling wine Wine containing carbon dioxide of fermentative origin that keeps bubbling after opening; traditional method, tank method and ancestral method are distinct, and Champagne is only one example. Sparkling wine Sparkling wine is wine that contains carbon dioxide and keeps producing bubbles after the bottle is opened. The bubbles may come from fermentation or from added gas. Under the OIV definition, true sparkling wine derives its carbon dioxide entirely from fermentation (endogenous origin) and has an excess pressure in the bottle of at least 3.5 bar at 20 °C. records.content: Spiced Rum A flavoured spirit made by adding spices, sugar and caramel to a rum base; common notes are vanilla, cinnamon, clove, nutmeg and orange peel, with styles from light to sweet and rich. records.content: Stout A top-fermented dark beer given colour and coffee-cocoa flavour by roasted barley, named after stronger porter, represented by Dublin dry stout and split into sweet, oatmeal and imperial stout. The name comes from 18th century “stout porter”, a stronger porter; in the 19th century Dublin developed the dry stout form, and in the 20th century sweet stout, oatmeal stout and imperial stout branched off. records.content: Tequila A Mexican spirit distilled from blue Weber agave, with 100% agave and mixto expressions and several age tiers. Tokaji Tokaji is the sweet wine of the Tokaj region in north-eastern Hungary, and one of the earliest sweet wine systems to be written into law. Its core is Aszú: botrytised grapes are picked by hand, macerated in base wine or fermenting must from the same vintage, then pressed, fermented and aged in oak for at least eighteen months. records.content: Triple Sec A clear orange liqueur made by macerating sweet and bitter orange peels in neutral spirit, distilling and sweetening; it is a style, not a brand, and its border with curaçao lies in base spirit, colour and sweetness. It is neither a protected trademark nor a single brand, but a style that took shape in nineteenth-century France and later became a fixture of cocktail culture. records.content: Vermouth An aromatised wine based on wine, flavoured with wormwood and other botanicals and fortified by category; EU rules set an actual-alcohol range from 14.5% up to but below 22% and a total-alcohol floor of 17.5%, and dry, white and red styles work almost like three different ingredients. Vermouth Vermouth is an aromatised wine: a wine base plus wormwood, clove, cinnamon, citrus peel and other botanicals, fortified according to product type and adjusted for sugar. It has the acidity and fruit of wine and the bitterness and aroma of a spirit, so it can be drunk alone or used in cocktails. records.content: Vin Santo A sweet Tuscan “holy wine” made from dried grapes and aged in wood for years; dried apricot, honey, nuts and caramel, traditionally served with cantucci almond biscuits. Vin Santo Vin Santo is a dried-grape wine of central Italy, above all Tuscany: grapes are dried in a ventilated space to concentrate sugar, fermented slowly, then aged for years in small wooden casks. records.content: Vodka A neutral spirit distilled from grain, potato, molasses or other agricultural materials, with more flavour variation than the "colourless and tasteless" stereotype suggests. Vodka Vodka is a neutral spirit made from agricultural materials such as grain, potato or molasses, then fermented, distilled and filtered or treated. records.content: Wheat beer A top-fermented beer made with a large share of wheat; German wheat beer is marked by clove and banana esters and bottle conditioning, Belgian witbier by orange peel and coriander, and American wheat ale is cleaner, with wheat shaping body, head and haze. Wheat beer Wheat beer is top-fermented beer in which wheat makes up a large share of the grain bill. German wheat beer is marked by clove and banana esters and bottle conditioning; Belgian witbier is seasoned with orange peel and coriander; American wheat ale is cleaner and more easy-drinking. records.content: Whisky A grain spirit distilled, then aged in oak, with Scottish, Irish, American and Japanese traditions and strict labelling rules. Whisky Whisky (spelled whiskey in Ireland and the United States) is a spirit made from grain by mashing, fermentation and distillation, then aged in oak. Grain, still, cask and local climate shape the flavour; regional rules determine which names such as "Scotch" and "bourbon" may legally be used. Whisky image Figure: Whisky. records.title: White wine
records.summary: Wine made from white grapes, or from destemmed dark grapes, usually without skin fermentation; acidity, aroma, lees and oak treatment together shape the style.
records.content: White wine Wine made from white grapes, or from destemmed dark grapes, usually without skin fermentation; acidity, aroma, lees and oak treatment together shape the style. White wine White wine is made from white grape varieties, or from destemmed dark varieties. Unlike red wine, white wine usually does not let the liquid stay in contact with skins for long, so it is pale in colour and low in tannin, with acidity and aroma as its main structural pillars. Its range is wide: from crisp, dry, drink-now wines to rich wines shaped by oak and lees, and to base wines for sparkling wine. records.title: Wine

records.content: Wine An alcoholic drink made by fermenting fresh grapes or grape must; colour, sweetness, bubbles and regional rules define its categories, while terroir and vintage are only some of the variables. Wine Wine is an alcoholic drink made by fermenting fresh grapes or grape must. The OIV definition requires it to come entirely from fresh grapes (crushed or not) or grape must through partial or complete alcoholic fermentation, with an actual alcoholic strength of at least 8.5% vol. Under specific climatic, soil, variety or local-tradition conditions, some regional rules allow the minimum total strength to fall to 7% vol. records.content: Yellow wine A traditional Chinese fermented grain wine, mainly rice-based; Shaoxing is its best-known protected origin. It uses rice (glutinous, japonica or indica) as the main material, with wheat qu, starter or red yeast for saccharification and fermentation, followed by pressing, clarification, pasteurisation and ageing. records.content: Acidity Acidity describes the amount and strength of acids in a drink, commonly through total acidity in g/L and pH, two different measures; it supports freshness, balance and ageing potential, and affects sulfur dioxide effectiveness. Acidity Acidity image Figure: Acidity. Image: Chemicalinterest, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons (source page). records.content: Alcohol by volume (ABV) ABV is the volume fraction of ethanol in a drink measured at 20 °C, usually written as % vol; it is a basic labelling and formulation parameter, not a quality score. Alcohol by volume (ABV) Alcohol by volume (ABV) describes the share of ethanol in a drink by volume. It is usually written as “% vol”: 12.5% vol means that, at 20 °C, every 100 volume units of the drink contain 12.5 volume units of pure ethanol. records.content: Angel's share The angel's share is the portion of a spirit lost through the cask wall during maturation; the Scotch whisky trade often cites about 2% a year, but the real rate depends on temperature, humidity, cask size and warehouse type, and is neither a precise constant nor a quality grade. Angel's share The angel's share is the portion of a spirit that evaporates into the air through the cask wall during maturation. The name is romantic, but the thing it describes is practical: an oak cask is not a sealed container, ethanol and water keep escaping over time, the volume falls and the strength may change. records.title: Appellation
records.summary: An appellation is a legal designation that binds a geographical area to production rules, such as French AOC/AOP, Italian DOC/DOCG, Spanish DO and EU PDO/PGI; i
records.content: Appellation An appellation is a legal designation that binds a geographical area to production rules, such as French AOC/AOP, Italian DOC/DOCG, Spanish DO and EU PDO/PGI; it states origin and rules, not a quality ranking. Appellation An appellation is a legal geographical designation: it ties the production of a product to a defined area and a set of rules, and only products made inside that area, under those rules, may use the name. France calls it appellation d'origine contrôlée (AOC), later extended as appellation d'origine protégée (AOP); Italy has DOC and DOCG, Spain has DO and DOCa, and at EU level the categories are PDO and PGI.Where information sits on a wine label: estate, appellati

records.title: Aroma
records.summary: is the volatile smell perceived by the nose, layered by origin into varietal, fermentation and maturation notes; it is not the same as flavour, and aroma is not
records.content: Aroma Aroma is the volatile smell perceived by the nose, layered by origin into varietal, fermentation and maturation notes; it is not the same as flavour, and aroma is not a synonym for bouquet. Aroma Aroma is the volatile smell perceived by the nose. It is the first piece of information in tasting and a key clue to a drink's type, condition and complexity. Aroma is not the same as flavour: aroma happens mainly in the nasal cavity, while flavour combines taste in the mouth with smell rising from the back of the throat. records.content: Barrel finishing Barrel finishing moves a drink from its main maturation container into a different cask for a further period to add or adjust flavour; it is secondary maturation, not full-term use of that cask, and not cask strength. Barrel finishing Barrel finishing (also called secondary maturation) moves a drink from its main maturation container into a different cask for a further period, to add, adjust or unify flavour. It describes a later stage, not full-term use of that cask. Finishing appears in whisky, wine and beer, but the purposes, timing and legal constraints differ.Barrel finishing image Figure: Barrel finishing. Blend A blend combines different varieties, vintages, sites or base wines into a final product. It is one of the most common operations in drinks production, not a synonym for adulteration or inferior goods. records.title: Brix
records.summary: Degrees Brix (°Brix) express the mass fraction of sucrose in a solution at 20 °C, where 1 °Brix is 1 g of sucrose per 100 g of solution; they measure sugar and
records.content: Brix Degrees Brix (°Brix) express the mass fraction of sucrose in a solution at 20 °C, where 1 °Brix is 1 g of sucrose per 100 g of solution; they measure sugar and soluble solids, not alcohol or sweetness. Brix Degrees Brix (°Brix, also written °Bx) are a unit of sugar concentration. The definition is specific: at 20 °C, 1 °Brix equals 1 gram of sucrose in 100 grams of solution, which is a sucrose mass fraction of 1%. Wine and juice producers use it to judge grape ripeness, estimate potential alcohol and monitor fermentation. Brix image Figure: Brix. records.title: Cask strength

records.content: Cask strength Cask strength means whisky bottled with little or no added water, retaining its natural strength from the cask, commonly around 50–65% vol; it is a bottling choice, not single cask or a quality grade. Cask strength Cask strength (also called natural strength) means whisky is bottled with little or no added water, retaining the alcohol by volume the liquid developed in the cask. It describes a bottling decision, not a cask type, an age or a quality grade. Cask-strength products commonly sit around 50%–65% vol, but two batches from the same distillery can differ by several degrees because each cask reaches its own natural strength. records.content: Chill filtration Chill filtration cools whisky or another spirit close to freezing so that long-chain fatty-acid esters, proteins and similar compounds precipitate and can be filtered out, mainly to prevent haze at low temperature or after dilution. It is an optional process, not a legal grade, and not the same as stripping all flavour. Chill filtration Chill filtration is an optional step before bottling whisky: the liquid is cooled close to freezing so that long-chain fatty-acid esters, fatty acids and proteins that were dissolved in the alcohol precipitate, and are then caught by a filter medium. records.title: Clos

records.content: Clos A clos is a vineyard plot enclosed by a wall, fence or natural boundary, common in Burgundy, the Loire and Alsace; it identifies a bounded site, is not a legal classification, and does not imply single ownership. Clos A clos is a French noun for a vineyard plot enclosed by a wall, fence, ditch or natural boundary. It answers "where is this site and where does it end", not "which quality tier does it belong to". In Burgundy a clos often appears together with a named climat; in the Loire, Alsace, Jura and Champagne it is likewise part of a place name. The key is to treat clos as a site identifier, not a quality badge.Clos thematic illustration Figure: thematic illustration for Clos. Image

records.content: Craft beer A small-scale, independent and tradition-minded beer production and consumption movement that emerged in the United States in the late 20th century; an industry and market concept, not a legal grade or a guarantee of quality. Craft beer Craft beer is a beer production and consumption movement that emerged in the United States in the late 20th century, centred on small, independent breweries that value tradition as well as experiment. It describes scale, ownership and process orientation. It is not a legal grade, not a single style, and not a promise of quality. Craft beer image Figure: Craft beer. records.content: Cuvée Cuvée can mean the earliest, gentlest juice from sparkling-wine pressing, or a batch blended from several base wines; in most regions it is not a legal grade and often serves as a product name. Cuvée Cuvée is an overworked French word. It has at least two technical meanings: the gentlest juice released first during sparkling-wine pressing, and a batch assembled from several base wines. On a label it often becomes simply a product name. The three meanings overlap, but none is a legal quality grade.Cuvée thematic illustration Figure: thematic illustration for Cuvée. records.title: Decanting
records.summary: moves wine from its bottle into another vessel for two purposes — separating sediment and exposing the wine to air; old reds and young tannic wines have differe
records.content: Decanting Decanting moves wine from its bottle into another vessel for two purposes — separating sediment and exposing the wine to air; old reds and young tannic wines have different goals, not every wine benefits, and timing depends on age and condition. Decanting Decanting means pouring wine slowly from its bottle into another vessel, usually a wide-bottomed glass decanter. The action has two purposes: separating the wine from sediment at the bottom of the bottle, and letting the wine contact air. Their conditions differ, and treating them as one leads to the mistaken conclusion that every wine should be decanted.Decanting thematic illustration Figure: thematic illustration for Decanting.

records.title: Disgorgement
records.summary: removes the yeast sediment from the neck of a traditional-method sparkling wine after riddling, by hand or with a frozen neck; dosage usually follows before the
records.content: Disgorgement Disgorgement removes the yeast sediment from the neck of a traditional-method sparkling wine after riddling, by hand or with a frozen neck; dosage usually follows before the final closure. Disgorgement Disgorgement (French dégorgement) is the step in traditional-method sparkling wine, after riddling, in which the yeast sediment gathered at the bottle neck is ejected. The sediment comes from the second fermentation in bottle: yeast converts sugar into alcohol and carbon dioxide, then dies and forms lees. records.title: Dosage

records.content: Dosage Dosage is the topping liquid added after disgorging traditional-method sparkling wine, usually a blend of base wine and sugar; it replaces the volume lost at disgorging and sets the finished sweetness class, from brut nature to doux under EU rules. Dosage Dosage is the small volume of liquid added to traditional-method sparkling wine after disgorging and before the final closure. It is usually a blend of the same base wine and sugar, known in French as liqueur d'expédition. The step has two jobs: replace the wine lost during disgorging, and set the finished sweetness class. records.title: Dry
records.summary: is a residual-sugar category on wine labels, usually no more than 4 g/L under EU rules and up to 9 g/L when acidity is high; it says nothing about fruit intensi
records.content: Dry Dry is a residual-sugar category on wine labels, usually no more than 4 g/L under EU rules and up to 9 g/L when acidity is high; it says nothing about fruit intensity or quality. Dry Dry is the word wine labels use for a very low level of sugar left after fermentation. It answers a narrow question: how much sugar remains? It does not say how intense, good or fruity the wine is. Reading dry as "no fruit" or "top quality" is one of the most common mistakes made at the shelf. records.content: Fermentation pit A solid-state fermentation vessel for baijiu, usually built from yellow mud, stone, brick, concrete or wood and often rectangular. Fermentation pit A fermentation pit is a solid-state fermentation vessel and one of the most recognisable facilities in baijiu production. records.content: Filtration Filtration passes wine through a medium that physically retains particles and microorganisms; depth and surface filtration differ in structure, and filtration affects clarity, stability and flavour but is not the same as fining. Filtration Filtration passes wine through a medium that physically retains suspended particles, yeast and bacteria. Its immediate aims are clarity and microbiological stability, not "filtering out flavour". records.title: Fining
records.summary: adds bentonite, egg white, gelatin or synthetic polymers to wine so that they adsorb suspended or dissolved targets and settle out, removing protein, tannin, co
records.content: Fining Fining adds bentonite, egg white, gelatin or synthetic polymers to wine so that they adsorb suspended or dissolved targets and settle out, removing protein, tannin, colour or off-flavours; it is a clarification and stabilisation step, not filtration, and raises vegan and allergen questions. Fining Fining is the addition of a small amount of an agent to wine so that it binds suspended or dissolved target substances, forms larger particles and settles, improving clarity and stability. It works through chemical reaction and adsorption; filtration works through physical retention. records.title: Finish
records.summary: is the taste, aroma and mouthfeel that persist after a drink is swallowed or spat out; length, layers and cleanliness determine its quality, and a long finish i
records.content: Finish Finish is the taste, aroma and mouthfeel that persist after a drink is swallowed or spat out; length, layers and cleanliness determine its quality, and a long finish is not a quality guarantee. Finish Finish (also called length, aftertaste or the tail) is the taste, aroma and mouthfeel that continue in the mouth and nose after a drink is swallowed or spat out. It is not the burst at the moment of swallowing but the fading curve over the following seconds to tens of seconds. In tasting, length, layers, cleanliness and direction together form the judgement, rather than an isolated number of seconds. Finish thematic illustration Figure: thematic illustration for Finish. records.content: Flor Flor is the yeast film that forms on the surface of Sherry during biological ageing, shielding the wine from oxygen and metabolising alcohol and glycerol; Fino and Manzanilla depend on flor, while Oloroso follows an oxidative route. Flor Flor is the layer of yeast film that forms on the surface of Sherry during biological ageing. In Spanish it is called velo de flor, the "veil of flowers". It is made up of several yeast strains, mainly within Saccharomyces; the film separates the wine from air while metabolising alcohol, glycerol and dissolved oxygen into acetaldehyde and related compounds. records.title: Heads, hearts and tails

records.content: Heads, hearts and tails A distillation run is split by volatility into heads, hearts and tails; hearts are the balanced middle cut and the body of the spirit, while heads and tails carry more impurities and are usually recycled, with cut points shaping style. Heads, hearts and tails Heads, hearts and tails are the three fractions of a pot-still run. They are not three different spirits but three successive parts of one distillation. The operator switches collection vessels according to aroma, taste and strength: heads come first, hearts in the middle, tails last. records.content: Hongqu A purple-red qu made by culturing Monascus on rice; it is a saccharifying starter for huangjiu, a colouring material and a base for red-qu wine and foods, with citrinin risk requiring process control. Hongqu Hongqu is a purple-red qu made by steaming rice, inoculating it with Monascus and culturing it. It is both a traditional saccharifying starter and a food colouring material. Within huangjiu it defines the red-qu huangjiu category, and it has separate uses in red-qu paste, red fermented bean curd and pigment production. records.content: IBU (International Bitterness Units) IBU is the unit for beer bitterness, with 1 IBU roughly equal to 1 milligram of iso-alpha acids per litre; it measures hop-derived bitterness, not the bitterness felt on the palate, and not hop aroma. IBU (International Bitterness Units) IBU (International Bitterness Units) is the unit the beer industry uses to quantify bitterness. 1 IBU is roughly 1 milligram of iso-alpha acids per litre of beer, or 1 ppm. It describes the concentration of hop-derived bitter compounds, not the bitterness intensity felt on the tongue at the moment of drinking. records.title: Late harvest
records.summary: is the practice of leaving grapes on the vine beyond normal ripeness so that water loss concentrates sugar and flavour; it can make sweet wine, but it is not th
records.content: Late harvest Late harvest is the practice of leaving grapes on the vine beyond normal ripeness so that water loss concentrates sugar and flavour; it can make sweet wine, but it is not the same as noble rot and not always sweet. Late harvest Late harvest (French vendange tardive) means leaving grapes on the vine beyond normal ripeness and picking them later. In the extra time, the fruit loses water through transpiration, sugar and flavour compounds concentrate, acidity falls, and the berries soften and darken. records.title: Lees
records.summary: are the solids, mostly spent yeast plus pulp residue and tartrates, that settle after fermentation; keeping fine lees and stirring them changes texture, aroma a
records.content: Lees Lees are the solids, mostly spent yeast plus pulp residue and tartrates, that settle after fermentation; keeping fine lees and stirring them changes texture, aroma and stability. Lees Lees are the solid matter that settles to the bottom of a vessel after fermentation ends. They consist mainly of spent yeast cells, along with grape pulp and skin residue, tartrates, proteins and a little other particulate matter. Lees are not a synonym for dirt, nor waste that must be removed at once; in winemaking they can add flavour and texture, and they can also cause faults. records.content: Malolactic fermentation A secondary fermentation in which lactic acid bacteria convert malic acid into lactic acid and carbon dioxide, softening acidity; it differs from alcoholic fermentation and is not needed in every wine. Malolactic fermentation Malolactic fermentation, usually shortened to MLF, is a secondary fermentation in winemaking, but the agent is not yeast. records.content: Mash A mash is the mixture of milled malt and hot water in a mash tun, where enzymes convert starch into fermentable sugar. Mash A mash is the thick mixture of milled malt, or grist, and hot water in a mash tun. It is not wort but the precursor of wort: starch granules gelatinise in the hot water, the malt's amylases cut starch into sugar, proteases break protein down, and a sugar- and amino-acid-rich liquid begins to form. Mousse Mousse is how the foam behaves after sparkling wine is poured into a glass: how the bubbles start, how coarse or fine they are, how thick the foam layer is and how long it lasts. Must Must is the juice obtained after crushing or pressing grapes, together with the pulp, skins, seeds and a little stem that remain suspended in it. records.content: Noble rot Noble rot is infection of ripe grapes by Botrytis cinerea under humid nights and dry, sunny days, which shrinks the fruit and concentrates sugar, acid and flavour; it makes Sauternes and Tokaji-style sweet wines but differs from grey rot in persistently wet conditions. Noble rot Noble rot is the outcome of Botrytis cinerea infecting ripe grapes under an alternating weather pattern: humid nights and mornings, then dry, sunny afternoons. It is not a single reaction but a chain: ethanol can be oxidised to acetaldehyde, phenolics to quinones, and pigments and tannin polymerise or brown along the way. records.content: Peat Peat is partially decomposed plant matter formed in oxygen-poor bogs, and its smoke deposits phenols on kilned malt; peatiness is an optional whisky style, not a required feature of all Scotch whisky. Peat Peat is partially decomposed plant matter that accumulates slowly in cold, wet, oxygen-poor bogs. When burned as fuel it releases heavy smoke and phenolic compounds; the whisky industry uses peat smoke to kiln malt so that phenols attach to the grain and then pass through mashing, fermentation and distillation. records.content: Tannin Tannins are a group of polyphenolic compounds that bind proteins and create astringency; in wine they come mainly from skins, seeds, stems and oak. records.content: Terroir Terroir is the combined effect of a place's natural conditions and long-standing human practice on the character of its produce; it is not a single soil measurement. records.content: Assyrtiko A white grape from Santorini in Greece that keeps high acidity in wind, drought and volcanic soil, giving dry wines of lemon, flint and sea salt, with Vinsanto as its sweet counterpart. records.content: Barbera A red grape of Piedmont in Italy with high acidity, medium tannin and deep colour, heat-tolerant and steady in yield, often contrasted with Nebbiolo as high acid against high tannin. Chardonnay Chardonnay is a major white grape variety, botanically Vitis vinifera. Genetic research shows that its parents are Pinot Noir and Gouais Blanc. Chardonnay has a fairly neutral aroma and high adaptability, which is why it is often called the winemaker's canvas: climate, soil, fermentation temperature, lees contact, malolactic fermentation and oak use all change the final style considerably.Chardonnay image Figure: Chardonnay. Heat- and drought-tolerant, vigorous and high-yielding, it has thin skins, pale colour, supple tannin and medium-high acidity, with red cherry, strawberry, white peach and floral notes. Dolcetto Dolcetto is one of Piedmont's three great red varieties in northwest Italy, alongside Nebbiolo and Barbera. The Italian name means "little sweet one", yet the wine is almost always dry. It ripens early with low acidity and tannin that can be gently extracted into a rounded frame; the colour is deep purple, with black cherry, plum, liquorice and a signature bitter-almond finish. Furmint Furmint is the most important white grape of Tokaj in Hungary and one of the most misunderstood varieties in the world. Most drinkers know it only through luscious botrytised sweet wine, yet the grape is high in acidity, thick-skinned and late-ripening, and can make dry whites of real tension. It is thin-skinned, early-ripening and high in acidity, and it is the core variety of Beaujolais red wine; it is also planted in France's Loire and elsewhere. records.content: Gewürztraminer An aromatic white grape with pink skins, named after Tramin in South Tyrol. An aromatic mutation of Savagnin, it is low in acidity and quick to accumulate sugar, known for lychee, rose, ginger and cinnamon, and grown mainly in Alsace, Germany, Austria and northern Italy. Gewürztraminer Gewürztraminer is one of the world's most recognisable white grapes: lychee, rose, ginger and cinnamon need almost no training to identify. That recognisability also brings misunderstanding, since many assume it must be sweet or that more aroma means better quality. Half of its story is in the vineyard, the other half in naming rules: until 2009 both grape and wine were called Prosecco, after which the variety officially became Glera while the wine kept the name Prosecco and the production area was redrawn. records.content: Grenache A heat- and drought-tolerant red grape with thin skins, fast sugar accumulation and low acidity, supporting fruit and alcohol in Rhône blends and in Spanish Priorat. DNA work confirms that Spain's Garnacha and Sardinia's Cannonau are the same variety. Grenache Grenache is one of the most important red grapes of the Mediterranean: heat- and drought-tolerant, quick to accumulate sugar, able to survive on dry, poor slopes. Its skins are thin, its tannin medium and its acidity low, so on its own it can feel loose, yet in blends it supplies fruit, alcohol and spice. It is neither a melon nor a Muscat, but a white grape native to Burgundy that became the leading variety around Nantes in the Loire Valley. Aromatic, with bright acidity and fine, moderate tannin, it shows black cherry, raspberry, violet, dried herb and slate mineral; from an obscure bulk blending grape in the late twentieth century it was revived into one of the most talked-about native reds of Iberia (ref:bierzo). records.content: Merlot A red grape common on Bordeaux's Right Bank, with medium berries, relatively thin skins and early ripening; its tannin and acidity are moderate, and it is used both as a varietal wine and in blends with Cabernet Sauvignon. Merlot Merlot is one of the most widely planted red grape varieties in the world and originated in Bordeaux, France. Its berries are medium in size, its skins relatively thin, and it ripens early; tannin and acidity are moderate, which is why it is often described as supple and easy to drink. records.content: Muscat Muscat is not one grape but a large, ancient family whose members share a striking floral and grapey aroma, ranging from dry Alsace white and lightly sparkling Italian Moscato to French and Australian fortified sweet wines. Muscat Muscat is not a single variety but an old and varied family of grapes spread across Europe and the Mediterranean. What unites it is aroma: orange blossom, grape, honey and citrus are usually obvious even in youth, and the wines rarely need age to be recognised. That aromatic power is why Muscat appears in almost every wine form—dry white, sweet white, lightly sparkling, fully sparkling, fortified sweet wine and even raisin wine. records.content: Pinot Blanc Pinot Blanc is a white mutation of Pinot Noir with moderate to high acidity and a gentle, rounded style, grown in Alsace (often blended with Auxerrois), Germany as Weissburgunder and northern Italy as Pinot Bianco, for still whites and sparkling wine. Pinot Blanc Pinot Blanc is the white member of the Pinot family, often described as a quiet white grape: its aroma is understated, its acidity moderate to high, its body rounded and its affinity with food broad. It performs consistently in Alsace, Germany and northern Italy, yet has long lived in the shadow of the more fashionable Chardonnay and Riesling. records.content: Pinot Gris A grey-skinned colour mutation of Pinot Noir, early-ripening, thin-skinned and low in acidity. Alsace can make it full and rich, while Italy makes it light and crisp as Pinot Grigio; the Italian delle Venezie DOC, created in 2017, expanded that style further. Pinot Gris Pinot Gris is a colour mutation of Pinot Noir, its fruit grey-pink rather than purple-black. It ripens early, has thin skins and low acidity, and usually gives a pale wine with pear and apple aromas. The same variety can be full and rich in Alsace or light and crisp in Italy, a difference driven mainly by region and winemaking rather than the grape itself. Pinot Gris image Figure: Pinot Gris. records.content: Pinot Meunier Pinot Meunier is the dark-skinned Pinot mutation that buds and ripens early, performs well on the clay slopes of the Marne Valley and gives Champagne red-fruit richness and roundness, whether in blends or in increasingly popular single-varietal and Blanc de Noirs bottlings. Pinot Meunier Pinot Meunier is the most underrated of Champagne's three main permitted varieties. It is a dark-skinned mutation of Pinot Noir, with dark grapes and white flesh, and it buds and ripens early, which makes it reliable on the clay slopes of the Marne Valley. records.title: Pinot Noir
records.summary: A thin-skinned, pale-coloured red grape with high acidity that is highly sensitive to climate and viticulture; it is the basis of red Burgundy and an important
records.content: Pinot Noir A thin-skinned, pale-coloured red grape with high acidity that is highly sensitive to climate and viticulture; it is the basis of red Burgundy and an important component of Champagne, spanning light fruit to complex aged styles. Pinot Noir Pinot Noir is one of the most difficult red varieties to grow and one of the most transparent to site. Its berries are small, its skins thin, its colour pale, its tannin fine and its acidity high. In Burgundy it shows detailed red fruit and minerality; in Champagne it is often a blending component for sparkling wine. Its style spans a wide range, from light and easy to complex and long-lived.Pinot Noir image Figure: Pinot Noir. Image: Cjp24, Pub

records.content: Pinotage A South African red grape created in 1925 by crossing Pinot Noir with Cinsaut at Stellenbosch, known for deep colour, firm tannin and a style that ranges from fresh fruit to coffee and smoke. Pinotage Pinotage is South Africa's own red grape and one of the few varieties bred in the 20th century to gain a distinct international identity. It was created by crossing Pinot Noir with Cinsaut, combining the smaller berries and aromatic potential of the former with the resilience and yield of the latter. records.content: Piquepoul A white grape of Languedoc, France, centred on Picpoul de Pinet; high acidity, lemon, sea salt and white flowers, it suits oysters and seafood and represents the Mediterranean “sea-air” white. Piquepoul Piquepoul (also Picpoul, Picapoll) is an ancient white grape of southern France's Languedoc, best expressed in Picpoul de Pinet AOP on the shores of the Étang de Thau. Late-ripening with naturally high acidity, it makes pale green-gold wines of lemon, green apple and white flower over a saline, iodine mineral note, the archetypal Mediterranean "sea-air" dry white, long matched with Bouzigues oysters and lagoon shellfish (ref:white). records.content: Riesling A high-acid, clearly aromatic white grape known for lime, green apple and, with age, mineral and petrol notes; Germany, Alsace and Austria are core regions, and sweetness ranges widely. records.content: Sauvignon Blanc An aromatic white grape known for citrus, grass, gooseberry and tropical notes; it has high acidity and suits cool regions, showing different faces in the Loire, Bordeaux and New Zealand. Sauvignon Blanc Sauvignon Blanc is one of the most aromatic white grape varieties. Its skins are relatively thin and its acidity high, and it often shows citrus, grass, gooseberry and tropical notes; cool regions make it fresh, while warm regions push it toward tropical fruit. records.content: Sémillon A Bordeaux white grape with thin skins and low acidity, prone to botrytis, the main variety of Sauternes and Barsac and also used for dry Graves white. It shows lemon, beeswax, honey and apricot, and in the 1855 classification Château d'Yquem was the only estate rated Premier Cru Supérieur. Sémillon Sémillon is the backbone white grape of Bordeaux and one of the world's most underrated whites. Thin-skinned, low in acidity and quick to accumulate sugar, it can make dry white wine as well as rich sweet wine under botrytis. Its strength is not high acid or loud aroma but texture, a waxy feel and the complexity that comes with age. Sémillon photograph Figure: Sémillon. Photograph: Sémil

Trebbiano Trebbiano is a name that misleads. It is both a group of white grapes widely planted in Italy and, in France, the grape the country calls Ugni Blanc, the mainstay of Cognac and Armagnac. The same variety is Trebbiano Toscano in Italy and Ugni Blanc in France, and it does completely different work in the two places: Italy uses it for light white wines and as a base for sweet wines, while France distils it into the world's best-known brandies. records.content: Viognier A white grape native to the Northern Rhône, with thicker skins, low acidity and intense aroma. records.content: Xinomavro A red grape from Naoussa in northern Greece, known for high acidity, firm tannin and tomato-olive notes, often called “the Greek Nebbiolo”; with age it gains leather, dried fruit and spice. Xinomavro Xinomavro (also spelled Xynomavro) is the most serious red grape of Greek Macedonia in the northern part of the country. Its name combines the Greek xino (acid) and mavro (black), meaning "sour black". High in acidity and phenols with firm tannin, it closes up when young and needs years in bottle to unfold red fruit, tomato, olive and dried herb layers; fine examples age for ten to thirty years, and the grape is often compared with Piedmont's Nebbiolo (ref:nebbiolo). records.content: Zinfandel A red grape native to Dalmatia in Croatia and genetically identical to Italy's Primitivo, brought to the United States in the 19th century and now the signature grape of California old vines and high-alcohol reds. Zinfandel Zinfandel is California's signature red grape and one of the few varieties that matters on both sides of the Atlantic. In Puglia, Italy, it is called Primitivo; on the Dalmatian coast of Croatia it survives under the older names Tribidrag and Crljenak Kaštelanski. Jammy blackberry, black pepper and high alcohol are its most familiar face, yet well-farmed old vines can show spice, dried herbs and a mineral edge. records.content: Zweigelt Austria’s most important red grape, a cross of Blaufränkisch and St. Laurent; early-ripening and high-yielding, deep in colour with low tannin, black cherry, spice and violet, best drunk young. Zweigelt Zweigelt is Austria's most planted red grape, bred in 1922 at Klosterneuburg by Fritz Zweigelt from Blaufränkisch and St. Laurent. It ripens early, crops well and tolerates cold; the wine is deep coloured with soft tannins, black cherry, violet and spice, spanning light young wines to oak-aged reserve bottlings.
